newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-GLITZ VS GRIT AS RIVALS KICK OFF.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-GLITZ VS GRIT AS RIVALS KICK OFF.

text.p: Media tycoon Rupert Murdoch's Super League competition will kick off in Australia on Saturday amid the fanfare of a multi-million dollar advertising campaign to win back a legion of disillusioned rugby league fans.
Two years after Murdoch launched his bid to start a rebel competition, the battle for control of the sport in Australia will finally move on to the playing field.

Super League's maiden season will kick off on Saturday when Brisbane Broncos play New Zealand visitors Auckland Warriors to give Murdoch a six-day headstart on the rival Australian Rugby League (ARL) premiership.

The match will be the culmination of a long battle by Murdoch to poach the game away from the ARL, the game's Australian rulers for the past 89 years, and make it part of his sports-driven global pay-television network.
Both sides have waged massive propaganda campaigns that reflect their contrasting styles and visions for the game: Super League glitz and glamour versus ARL grit and tradition.
"We certainly want to protect the traditions of the game but we want to get the young people back," Super League chief executive John Ribot said at his competition's campaign launch.
"This is a youth (advertising) campaign, a family campaign, it's about entertainment and getting the fun back into rugby league," he said.

ARL chief executive Neil Whittaker in turn urged fans to look past slick television presentations and embrace a game which had been followed by generations in Australia, the world's strongest playing nation.
"People should get to the grounds and protect what is theirs," Whittaker said at the ARL's launch this week.

"Debate the bells and whistles all you like, rugby league comes down to who has the players and the clubs...Ninety years of tradition gives us an enormous position of strength...We're not in this for profit. That's the fundamental difference."
The battle for control of the game not only split the code, it saw rugby league lose ground to two other Australian winter sports, rugby union and Australian Rules football.

As a consequence the rival camps had to fight to win back the hearts and wallets of fans in advertising battles which have pitted the glitz of Murdoch's Super League dilettantes against the grit of the blue-collar ARL loyalists.
Super League fired the opening salvo on February 4 with its slick A$10 million (US$7.7 million) "Two Tribes" campaign based on a song by cult band Frankie Goes To Hollwood.
The ARL responded with its A$5 million "It's My Game" drive aimed directly at long-time but alienated fans.
Both sides are confident their strategies have been correct, that they will ultimately outlive their rivals in a market which each agrees can sustain only one premiership.
Prominent Australia and Canberra Raiders player Laurie Daley said Super League players and officials had fought with passion to create a "new brand" of rugby league.
"It was a passion to make our game better, to provide a standard of competition that we can be proud of and to take the game of rugby league to the international level where it belongs," Daley said.
The battle over rugby league claimed many victims, not the least of them outgoing ARL chairman Ken Arthurson, who resigned last month citing declining health after 14 years in charge.
"We've been done and dusted so many times it's not funny," Arthurson said. "I have no doubt that it is an era that will see the ARL push ahead."
The protracted courtroom battle also meant Australia lagged behind Europe, where Super League began last year after England's Rugby Football League wholeheartedly embraced Murdoch's plans.
Super League won the legal battle late last year when an appeal in Australia's Federal Court was upheld, overruling an earlier decision banning Murdoch's "rebels" until 2000.
